rv.q: The vulnerability behind what it takes to go big or go home is the secret, beating heart of "KPOP," a pulse that brings life to every chorus of its playlist.
But the paper-thin characterizations and hackneyed dialogue don’t prevent KPOP from being great fun.
The show is at its best when it leans into the spectacle, delivering the kind of high-energy performance that makes K-pop so magnetic in the first place.
The musical 'KPOP' on Broadway is a spectacle that dazzles with its choreography and energy, even if the book doesn't quite match the ambition of its production values.
It’s still exciting, sometimes thrilling — but it’s a packaged entertainment rather than an adventure in theater.

For them, the musical is less an eye-opener than an ear-pounder, assiduously drowning out any ambitions it may once have had to be more.
The show is visually spectacular and the performers are undeniably talented, but the book is thin and the songs, while energetic, lack the melodic sophistication that would make them memorable.
It feels as if the show has rushed out into the open water of Broadway and then gotten stuck, like a ship unable to catch the wind.
And, frankly, it lands somewhere in the uncertain middle, likely satisfying none of these demands.
It is also, unfortunately, a lesson of KPOP itself, which has now arrived at Broadway's Circle in the Square with so much plastic surgery that it is barely recognizable.
The musical captures the slick professionalism and manufactured glamour of the K-pop industry, but struggles to find its own authentic voice beneath the glossy surface.
The musical's book, by Jason Kim, offers a behind-the-scenes look at the pressures and artifice of the K-pop industry, but the storytelling feels as manufactured as the pop confections it depicts.
KPOP The Musical is the most exciting, interesting, and alive show on Broadway right now.

What makes “KPOP” transcend buoyant entertainment is its focus on the tensions underlying the exhilarating, dazzlingly precise song-and-dance routines on display here, courtesy of composer/lyricists Helen Park and Max Vernon and choreographer Jennifer Weber.

On the other hand, KPOP, written by Jason Kim and directed by Teddy Bergman, has scarcely enough compelling substance to sustain its own first act.
All of this spells doom for KPOP, a delightful musical entertainment that is best appreciated as just that, and nothing more.
But when the company sings the final song, "Blast Off," you may realize that you're having too much fun to notice–or care.
Like the genre it celebrates, “KPOP” works best when you let yourself get caught up in the sensation of the music and the precision dance moves — and try not to think too deeply.
In contrast, its attempt at drama feels like meager filler, and unconvincingly glued on to the more music-y musical the production seems to be straining to be.
Which begs the question: with so many actual K-pop acts now appearing in the area on a regular basis, why not go for the real thing instead of a highly proficient reproduction?
If this is the future of Broadway, please consider me a rabid and reinvigorated stan.
See the show, and you’ll understand why K-pop and its stars have taken over the musical universe.
The production numbers bring the house down, but there’s not much else there.
Well, you might be better off at home.
But, in its journey to Midtown, a reimagined KPOP has abandoned its weightier self-awareness, along with a lot of its creativity.
I cannot think of a show that, in its commercial transfer, has managed so thoroughly to shed so much of its stardust.
